record.paper_title: Theoretical descriptions of compound-nuclear reactions: open problems & challenges
record.original_question: Which theoretical developments missing from widely used Hauser-Feshbach-based reaction codes, and which underlying assumptions of those descriptions, must be implemented or tested in order to obtain reliable and comprehensive descriptions of compound-nuclear reactions?

evidence.quote: Despite the wide use of the Hauser-Feshbach formalism in modern reaction codes, some of the available theoretical developments have not yet been implemented and some of the underlying assumptions remain to be tested.

We find that various questions and challenges remain to be addressed in order to gain a deeper understanding of the many-body processes involved and to obtain reliable, comprehensive descriptions of this important class of nuclear reactions.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the standard Hauser–Feshbach statistical formalism used to describe compound-nuclear reactions. In this framework, a reaction proceeding through an equilibrated compound nucleus is described by an average cross section of the form

  σ_{ab}(E) = (π/k_a^2) Σ_J (2J+1)/[(2I_1+1)(2I_2+1)] · ⟨T_a^J T_b^J / Σ_c T_c^J⟩ · W_{ab}^J(E),

where T_c^J are transmission coefficients for entrance/exit channels c, W_{ab}^J is a width-fluctuation correction factor, and the sum extends over conserved quantum numbers (total angular momentum J, parity, etc.). The evaluation of these cross sections in modern reaction codes relies on a set of ingredients and assumptions, including: (i) optical-model transmission coefficients for particle channels; (ii) nuclear level densities ρ(E,J,π) used to model the continuum of compound and residual states; (iii) γ-ray strength functions f_{XL}(E_γ) governing radiative channels; (iv) width-fluctuation corrections (e.g. of Moldauer or GOE type) accounting for correlations between entrance and exit channels; (v) the Bohr independence hypothesis (factorization of formation and decay of the compound nucleus); (vi) statistical assumptions on the distribution of resonance widths and spacings (Porter–Thomas, Wigner GOE statistics); (vii) treatment of pre-equilibrium and direct-reaction contributions and their coherent/incoherent interplay with the compound-nucleus mechanism; (viii) treatment of isospin mixing, parity dependence of level densities, and angular-momentum coupling; (ix) the surrogate-reaction approach for inferring (n,x) cross sections on unstable targets.

Identify and characterize, in a precise and systematic manner, which theoretical developments among the items above (and related ones) are missing from current implementations of Hauser–Feshbach reaction codes, and which of the underlying assumptions remain untested. Specify which of these must be incorporated or rigorously validated in order to obtain reliable, comprehensive predictions of compound-nuclear reaction observables (cross sections, spectra, angular distributions) across the nuclear chart, including for nuclei far from stability.
artifact.status_search_result: This is a broad open-problems question about nuclear-reaction theory. Reviews and community white papers since 2014 (e.g., FRIB Theory Alliance reports, FRIB-TA topical programs on statistical nuclear reactions, and ongoing work on width fluctuations, level densities, and surrogate reactions) consistently identify the same set of open issues — width-fluctuation corrections beyond Moldauer, validity of Bohr's independence hypothesis, level-density and γ-strength uncertainties, pre-equilibrium/direct-compound interference, and surrogate-reaction modeling — as still unresolved. No comprehensive resolution exists; the problem remains open.

status_evidence.claim: Major ingredients of Hauser–Feshbach modeling remain active research topics with unresolved theoretical issues.
